experiments.name: Rutherford Gold Foil (1909)
experiments.summary: Alpha particles fired at gold foil. Most pass through, a few bounce straight back.
experiments.what_it_proved: Atoms are mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.
experiments.surprise: Before Rutherford, the 'plum pudding' model had electrons embedded in a diffuse positive charge. The bounce-back result was, in Rutherford's words, 'almost as incredible as if you fired 15-inch shells at tissue paper and they came back.'

experiments.name: Millikan Oil Drop (1909)
experiments.summary: Charged oil droplets suspended between charged plates. Electric force balances gravity at exactly integer multiples of a base charge.
experiments.what_it_proved: Electric charge is quantized — electrons have a fixed elementary charge of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
experiments.surprise: Nobody knew if charge could be fractional. This showed charge only comes in discrete packets.

experiments.name: Bohr Hydrogen Spectrum (1913)
experiments.summary: Hydrogen gas glows with exact discrete wavelengths — not a continuous rainbow.
experiments.what_it_proved: Electrons occupy quantized energy levels. Emitting a photon = electron dropping to a lower level.
experiments.surprise: Classical physics predicted atoms should continuously emit radiation and collapse. Quantized orbits explained why atoms are stable.

experiments.name: Discovery of Radium (1898)
experiments.summary: Processed tons of pitchblende ore to isolate milligrams of two new radioactive elements.
experiments.what_it_proved: Radioactivity is an atomic property, not a molecular one. New elements could be identified by their radiation.
experiments.surprise: Marie hand-carried samples in her pockets. Her notebooks are still radioactive and stored in lead-lined boxes in Paris.

experiments.name: Chadwick's Neutron (1932)
experiments.summary: Beryllium bombarded with alpha particles produced a penetrating radiation that could knock protons out of paraffin wax.
experiments.what_it_proved: Neutrons exist — neutral particles of almost identical mass to protons.
experiments.surprise: Filled the gap: nuclei contain protons AND neutrons, explaining why atomic mass ≈ 2× atomic number for most elements.

experiments.name: Moseley's X-Ray Law (1913)
experiments.summary: X-ray frequencies from different elements follow a precise law tied to their atomic number, not atomic weight.
experiments.what_it_proved: Atomic number (proton count) is the fundamental property of an element — not mass.
experiments.surprise: Predicted the existence of 4 missing elements (gaps at 43, 61, 72, 75). All were later found. Moseley was killed at Gallipoli at age 27.

experiments.name: Nuclear Fission Discovery (1938)
experiments.summary: Uranium bombarded with neutrons produced barium — a much lighter element. The nucleus had split.
experiments.what_it_proved: Nuclei can split, releasing enormous energy (E=mc²). The mass difference converts to ~200 MeV per fission.
experiments.surprise: Hahn was the chemist who discovered it; Meitner (exiled to Sweden) was the physicist who explained it. He won the Nobel; she did not.

experiments.name: Law of Conservation of Mass (1789)
experiments.summary: Burned mercury in a sealed container. The ash weighed MORE than the mercury — equal to what oxygen the air lost.
experiments.what_it_proved: Mass is conserved in chemical reactions. Matter cannot be created or destroyed, only rearranged.
experiments.surprise: Overthrew phlogiston theory. Renamed 'dephlogisticated air' to 'oxygen.' Guillotined during the French Revolution in 1794.

experiments.name: Voltaic Pile (1800)
experiments.summary: Alternating discs of zinc, copper, and brine-soaked cardboard produce a steady electric current.
experiments.what_it_proved: Chemical reactions can produce electricity. Redox reactions drive electron flow.
experiments.surprise: The first battery enabled electrolysis — Davy immediately used it to isolate sodium and potassium (1807), elements that had never existed in pure form.
